samples.summary: `ctx switch` calls `process.exit(1)` immediately after `console.error(errorEnvelope(...))`, which can truncate the envelope when stderr is a pipe
samples.evidence: `console.error(errorEnvelope('NOT_LOGGED_IN', …)); process.exit(1);` (ctx.ts:96-108, and again at 113-116). On POSIX, `process.stderr` writes to a *pipe* are asynchronous (libuv-queued); `process.exit()` does not flush them, so an agent that captures stderr through a pipe — the exact consumer this change adds the machine-readable envelope for — can observe exit code 1 with no body at all. Every other emitter in the change (`outputError`, `schema`'s miss) sets `process.exitCode` and returns instead, which is flush-safe. Note the sibling `ctx list` uses `outputError` (no `process.exit`), so the two subcommands differ in whether the body survives.

samples.summary: `ctx list` and `status` still emit unattributed envelopes, so `error.command` is present or absent depending on which subcommand ran
samples.evidence: `ctx.ts:85` is `outputError(e)` and `status.ts:69` is `outputError(e)` — both left without the acting `Command` while every other action in the change passes `this`. The stated contract (and the new test comment "the code an agent branches on must not depend on which `ctx` subcommand it happened to run") is broken for the attribution field itself: `ctx switch` failures carry `command: 'ctx.switch'`, `ctx list`'s `NOT_LOGGED_IN` carries none.

samples.summary: `clearAuthCookies` sweeps the bare names but never the `__Host-` names when the deployment is currently non-Secure, so the asymmetry it documents is only handled in one direction
samples.evidence: `new Set([sessionCookieName(), refreshCookieName(), ...UNPREFIXED_SESSION_COOKIE_NAMES])`. When `useSecureCookies()` is false, `sessionCookieName()` === `'wafflebase_session'`, so the Set collapses to the two bare names and `__Host-wafflebase_session` / `__Host-wafflebase_refresh` are never expired. A deployment that turns `Secure` back off (e.g. `COOKIE_SECURE=true` removed, or an https callback URL replaced) leaves the previously-issued `__Host-` session and refresh JWTs in the browser permanently — sign-out cannot reach them, contradicting the method's own docstring ("in every shape this deployment may have written them") and the new test title ("sign-out expires every cookie shape"), which only exercises the production direction.

samples.summary: The new CLI refusal is delivered only to the browser; `wafflebase login` still hangs for the full (now longer) callback timeout, which is the opposite of the stated rationale
samples.evidence: `assertCliLoginAvailable()` throws `BadRequestException` on `GET /auth/github?mode=cli`, whose response goes to the browser. Its docstring says the 400 is preferable to a silent downgrade "because the person running `wafflebase login` is waiting on a loopback callback that would otherwise never arrive and would time out five minutes later with nothing to act on" — but after the 400 the loopback callback still never arrives, so the terminal still waits out `CALLBACK_TIMEOUT_MS`, which this same change raised from 180_000 to 300_000 (login.ts:516). The refusal is never surfaced to the waiting CLI process at all.

samples.summary: `cliLoginAvailable()` deliberately allows the `NODE_ENV=production`, no-callback-URL install; on a cleartext origin that yields an endless confirmation-page loop, not a fail-closed refusal
samples.evidence: `cliLoginAvailable()` returns `useSecureCookies() || loopbackCallback()`, and with `NODE_ENV=production` and no `GITHUB_CALLBACK_URL`/`COOKIE_SECURE`, `isSecureCookie()` returns true (oauth-state.ts:239). The docstring claims that if such an origin is actually cleartext "the browser discards the cookie and the gate fails closed rather than open". It does not fail closed in any usable sense: `CliLoginConfirmMiddleware` sets a `Secure` `__Host-wafflebase_cli_confirm` cookie the browser drops, so the clicked `?confirm=` never matches (middleware.ts:141-160) and the middleware re-renders a fresh confirmation page on every click — an unbounded loop with no diagnostic, until the CLI's five-minute timeout fires.

samples.summary: Handing the browser a loopback URL that 302s cross-site to the backend risks `Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site` on the CLI start, which `assertCliStartNotCrossSite` rejects with a 400
samples.evidence: `await deps.openBrowser(armLaunch(oauthUrl))` now opens `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/launch/<tok>`, which redirects (login.ts:664-669) to `${server}/auth/github?mode=cli…`. The backend refuses any `mode=cli` start whose `Sec-Fetch-Site` is not `none`/`same-origin`/`same-site` (github-auth.guard.ts:309-319). Fetch-metadata computes the header over the whole redirect chain; the `none` short-circuit for initiator-less navigations is what keeps this working, and it is browser-implementation-dependent (and does not hold if any opener/browser attributes an initiator to an externally launched URL). If any supported browser recomputes to `cross-site` across the loopback→backend hop, every `wafflebase login` 400s. No test covers the header on the post-redirect request.

samples.summary: `login-url.txt` is a single fixed path shared by all logins, so two concurrent non-TTY logins clobber and prematurely delete each other's URL
samples.evidence: `const file = join(dirname(getConfigPath()), 'login-url.txt')` — no per-attempt suffix. A second `wafflebase login` overwrites the first's URL, and when the first login settles its `finally` block (`if (urlFile) rmSync(urlFile, { force: true })`, login.ts:365) deletes the file the second login just told the user to open. The second user is then pointed at a nonexistent path with no way to reach their pending login.

samples.summary: Availability is asserted before the port is parsed, so `?mode=cli` with no/invalid port now 400s instead of degrading to a browser login
samples.evidence: `if (isCliStart) { this.assertCliStartNotCrossSite(req); this.assertCliLoginAvailable(); }` runs before `const port = parseCliPort(req.query?.port)`. `CliLoginConfirmMiddleware` still documents the opposite for that shape ("Not a usable CLI request. The guard ignores it too, so it falls through to an ordinary browser login", middleware.ts:129-131). On a non-secure deployment a bare `/auth/github?mode=cli` (or one with a junk port) is now a hard 400 telling the user to serve over https, where it previously completed as an ordinary browser sign-in.

samples.summary: `runCli` registers a `preAction` hook on every invocation, so hooks accumulate when the same program object is reused
samples.evidence: `program.hook('preAction', …)` is executed inside `runCli`, not in `buildProgram`. Calling `runCli(program)` more than once on one `Command` (as the tests do with a shared program) attaches N hooks that all fire per action. Harmless today because each writes the same `acting`, but it is a per-call side effect on a long-lived object.

samples.summary: Two of the new login tests do not set `WAFFLEBASE_CONFIG`, so `announceLoginUrl` writes and deletes `login-url.txt` in the developer's real `~/.wafflebase`
samples.evidence: Only the first test sets `process.env.WAFFLEBASE_CONFIG = configPath`; the `afterEach` deletes it, and the 'rejected exchange' and '5xx' tests set only `WAFFLEBASE_SESSION`. `announceLoginUrl` then resolves `dirname(getConfigPath())` to the real `~/.wafflebase`, creating it if absent and `rmSync`-ing `login-url.txt` there — a test touching the user's real config directory.

finding.summary: `ctx switch` calls `process.exit(1)` immediately after `console.error(errorEnvelope(...))`, which can truncate the envelope when stderr is a pipe
finding.evidence: `console.error(errorEnvelope('NOT_LOGGED_IN', …)); process.exit(1);` (ctx.ts:96-108, and again at 113-116). On POSIX, `process.stderr` writes to a *pipe* are asynchronous (libuv-queued); `process.exit()` does not flush them, so an agent that captures stderr through a pipe — the exact consumer this change adds the machine-readable envelope for — can observe exit code 1 with no body at all. Every other emitter in the change (`outputError`, `schema`'s miss) sets `process.exitCode` and returns instead, which is flush-safe. Note the sibling `ctx list` uses `outputError` (no `process.exit`), so the two subcommands differ in whether the body survives.

verdict.reason: The code is present exactly as claimed: ctx.ts:96-108 and ctx.ts:113-116 each call console.error(errorEnvelope(...)) and then process.exit(1) with no flush. Both branches sit on the ordinary `ctx switch` path (no session, line 94-95; unresolvable query, line 111-112) and nothing guards or pre-validates them. The claimed contrast holds: outputError sets process.exitCode and returns (formatter.ts:161-162), forwardUpstreamError does the same (formatter.ts:388-389), and the sibling `ctx list` routes through outputError (ctx.ts:85), so the two subcommands genuinely differ in whether the envelope body is guaranteed to be emitted. The reviewer's mechanism is imprecise — Node stdio pipe writes are synchronous on Linux/Windows and only asynchronous on macOS, and libuv attempts an inline write first, so a ~90-byte envelope usually escapes — which narrows the failure window but does not eliminate it; process.exit() does not flush pending stdio writes. No named refutation ground applies: the code is present, reachable, unguarded, and loss of the machine-readable error body is a correctness/data-loss concern in this lane.

finding.summary: Handing the browser a loopback URL that 302s cross-site to the backend risks `Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site` on the CLI start, which `assertCliStartNotCrossSite` rejects with a 400
finding.evidence: `await deps.openBrowser(armLaunch(oauthUrl))` now opens `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/launch/<tok>`, which redirects (login.ts:664-669) to `${server}/auth/github?mode=cli…`. The backend refuses any `mode=cli` start whose `Sec-Fetch-Site` is not `none`/`same-origin`/`same-site` (github-auth.guard.ts:309-319). Fetch-metadata computes the header over the whole redirect chain; the `none` short-circuit for initiator-less navigations is what keeps this working, and it is browser-implementation-dependent (and does not hold if any opener/browser attributes an initiator to an externally launched URL). If any supported browser recomputes to `cross-site` across the loopback→backend hop, every `wafflebase login` 400s. No test covers the header on the post-redirect request.

verdict.reason: The snippets exist as quoted, but the claimed failure (the loopback→backend redirect hop being 400'd by assertCliStartNotCrossSite) is unreachable. CliLoginConfirmMiddleware is registered on GET auth/github (auth.module.ts:45-49) and Nest middleware runs before guards; for a mode=cli request with a valid port and no `confirm` — exactly the shape armLaunch's 302 produces (login.ts:658-670, 826-830) — the middleware renders the confirmation page and returns without next() (cli-login-confirm.middleware.ts:162-171), never inspecting Sec-Fetch-Site. So GitHubAuthGuard.canActivate never runs on the post-redirect request, and whatever the browser computes over the redirect chain cannot 400 the flow. The only CLI-flow request that reaches assertCliStartNotCrossSite (github-auth.guard.ts:309-319) is the Continue click, a same-origin navigation to the relative href built at cli-login-confirm.middleware.ts:197/234, which is in ALLOWED_FETCH_SITES (guard.ts:129). The two middleware fall-through paths do not resurrect it: port===undefined (middleware.ts:128-132) is unreachable from the CLI, which always supplies an ephemeral port ≥1024 (login.ts:801,829 with parseCliPort at guard.ts:149-154), and !cliLoginAvailable() (middleware.ts:121-123) is a deployment that already refuses CLI login with a 400 (guard.ts:239-252), where a cross-site header only changes which refusal message is shown. The missing-test point is test coverage, outside the correctness lens.

finding.summary: Spawn-time `error` may still crash the CLI: the ordering claim the new comment relies on is unverified for `open`'s default `wait: false` path
finding.evidence: The delta's new comment (test/login-callback.test.ts:172-177) and the helper doc (src/commands/login.ts:101-113) both rest on the claim that `open` v11 attaches `once('error', reject)` in the same synchronous turn as `spawn()` ("index.js: spawn at :255, listener at :301, no await between them"), so a missing-opener ENOENT surfaces as a rejection caught by the `try` at login.ts:119. In every `open` release I can recall (v8-v10) that `once('error', reject)` lives **only inside the `if (options.wait)` branch**; with the default `wait: false` (which is what `openBrowser` uses — `open(url)` with no options, login.ts:121) `baseOpen` does `subprocess.unref(); return subprocess;` with no error listener at all. If that is still true in v11, the ENOENT that `child_process.spawn` schedules on `process.nextTick` is emitted onto an emitter with no `error` listener, and the nextTick queue drains before our promise continuation, so `child?.on?.('error', ...)` at login.ts:122 is attached too late — the unhandled `error` event becomes an uncaughtException and takes the CLI down mid-login on exactly the headless boxes this helper exists to survive. I could not confirm either way: `node_modules` is not present in the tree (pnpm-lock.yaml:7756 pins `open@11.0.0`), so the cited line numbers :255/:301 are unverifiable from the repo, and neither test exercises the real ordering — one mocks a resolved child and emits synchronously afterwards (test:187-196), the other mocks a rejection (test:198-204), so both pass regardless of which branch `open` actually takes. Someone should read node_modules/open/index.js and, if the listener is inside the `wait` branch, either pass `{wait: true}`-equivalent handling or attach the `error` handler via a wrapper that owns the spawn.

verdict.reason: The code is present exactly as the finding describes: openBrowser (login.ts:118-126) calls open(url) with no options (default wait:false) and attaches the 'error' listener only after the await (login.ts:122), while the doc comment (login.ts:101-113) and the test comment (login-callback.test.ts:168-181) both rest on the unverified claim that open v11 attaches once('error', reject) synchronously with spawn and resolves on 'spawn'. I could not verify that claim from this repository: node_modules is absent (Glob for **/node_modules/open/index.js returns nothing) and pnpm-lock.yaml:7771 / :17083 only pin open@11.0.0 with a dependency set (is-in-ssh, powershell-utils, wsl-utils) that differs from older releases, so the cited :255/:301 lines cannot be checked. No guard elsewhere makes the path unreachable: the try/catch at login.ts:119-125 catches rejections only, not an unhandled 'error' event, and there is no process-level safety net (no uncaughtException/unhandledRejection handler anywhere in packages/cli/src; bin.ts:6 is a bare void runCli() and cli.ts:84 is only a try around command parsing). The tests cannot settle it either — open is module-mocked at login-callback.test.ts:21 and both cases (test:187-196 resolved emitter, test:198-204 rejection) pass regardless of which branch real open takes. If the listener is indeed confined to the wait branch, a spawn-time ENOENT on a headless host becomes an uncaughtException that kills the CLI mid-login, which is a critical correctness/missing-guard defect in this lens. Since I have no named ground to refute (code present, no guard to cite, in-lane), the finding stands.

mergedFrom.summary: `openBrowser` attaches the child `error` listener too late to catch a failed spawn

finding.summary: `openBrowser` attaches the child `error` listener after `await`, which may be too late to prevent an uncaught exception

verdict.reason: The code is present exactly as described: packages/cli/src/commands/login.ts:121-122 does `const child = await open(url); child?.on?.('error', () => {});`, attaching the `error` listener only in the post-await continuation, and the doc comment at login.ts:101-113 states absorbing the spawn-time async `error` is the helper's purpose. The reviewer's critique of the test is also accurate: packages/cli/test/login-callback.test.ts:21 mocks the entire `open` module and :187-196 resolves a hand-built EventEmitter then emits `'error'` after `openBrowser` returned, so the real spawn/nextTick ordering is never exercised. Whether this is an actual crash depends on open@11.0.0's internals (pinned at pnpm-lock.yaml:7771): the in-repo comments claim v11 attaches `once('error', reject)` synchronously with the spawn and resolves on `'spawn'` (making the missing-binary case a rejection caught by the `try`), while the finding claims the v10 shape (`spawn(); unref(); return subprocess;`) leaves the nextTick error unhandled. node_modules is not installed and no vendored copy of `open` exists in the tree (`**/node_modules/open/index.js` and `**/open/package.json` both return no matches), so I have no in-repository evidence to refute the ordering claim. If real, an unhandled `'error'` event kills the CLI mid-login on a headless box, which is a blocking correctness defect. Uncertainty about the third-party internals means the finding stays.
